# Executive summary

This paper specifies the finite latent-progress extension to JoiNMe. JoiNMe
models multivariate longitudinal outcomes through nested mixed effects and can
jointly model a time-to-event process through current-value, current-slope,
correlation and covariance associations. The extension introduces
heterogeneity by replacing the centred distribution of selected standardised
random effects with a finite location--scale mixture.

The implementation has six defining properties.

Interpretive qualifications, analysis review and manuscript guidance are
maintained separately in
[JoiNMe interpretation and reporting notes](joinme-reporting-notes.qmd).

1. The public entry point is `joinme_mix()`, with fitted and predicted
   subclasses that inherit the existing JoiNMe interface.
2. Two latent-progress coordinates are selected per block by default.
3. Classes are attached to random-effect allocation units: subjects for
   subject and covariance-regression effects, markers for marker effects and
   marker weights.
4. Combining levels retains \(G\) classes. Compatible blocks share one
   allocation rather than producing a Cartesian product.
5. Discrete allocations are marginalised exactly in Stan.
6. A longitudinal-only form, available from both `joinme()` and
   `joinme_mix()`, removes the survival likelihood exactly whilst retaining
   the common model-building infrastructure.

The model has a direct generative implementation through
`simulate_joinme_mix()`. This simulator samples the otherwise marginalised
class allocations, generates selected standardised latent coordinates from
their component distributions, and delegates all remaining longitudinal and
event generation to `simulate_joinme()`. Simulation and fitting therefore
share their formula parsing, coordinate selection, allocation domains and
component-family convention.

The result is a bespoke but restrained extension. It changes the random-effect
distribution without duplicating the longitudinal likelihood, survival
likelihood, transformations, prediction programme or diagnostics.

# Scientific motivation

Multivariate longitudinal data often show more heterogeneity than a single
elliptical random-effect distribution can express. Two subjects may have
similar observed values at baseline but differ systematically in their
long-term direction. Conversely, two subjects may have similar mean
trajectories but markedly different covariance or volatility patterns.
Markers can also form classes according to their population deviations or
their importance in a survival association.

A finite latent-progress distribution offers a probabilistic description of
such heterogeneity. It is preferable to classifying estimated random effects
after model fitting for three reasons.

- Longitudinal measurement error and shrinkage are propagated into class
  uncertainty.
- Survival information can contribute to estimation when a joint model is
  fitted.
- Class locations, scales, proportions and random effects are estimated
  jointly rather than in a sequential plug-in procedure.

The word *latent* is important. A class is an unobserved component of a
statistical distribution, not an observed diagnosis. Posterior allocation
probabilities, sensitivity analysis and predictive assessment are therefore
central to interpretation.

# Generative latent-progress simulation

## Simulation-to-fit correspondence

### Population parameters and conditional realisations

Every population coefficient is fixed within a simulated data set and is
declared through the scientific components of `jm_truth()`. A finite numeric
vector fixes the coefficient vector exactly. A `prior_*()` declaration inside
`jm_truth()` defines a between-data-set generating distribution and the
simulator draws the coefficient vector once. The realised vector does not vary
by subject, marker or observation. Longitudinal and event coefficients,
association coefficients, distributional and formula-based baseline-hazard
coefficients, marker-weight means, and covariance-regression coefficients all
follow this principle.
Conditional quantities—random effects, marker-weight departures, responses,
event times and class allocations—are drawn given those population values.

The coefficients in `formulaClass` obey the same rule through
`truth$class$slope`. Numeric values fix the multinomial-logit coefficients;
`prior_*()` declarations generate them once and define their recovery prior.
Baseline probabilities, component locations and component scales remain the
generative mixture quantities in `class_parameters`.

A bare component declaration uses complete model-matrix order for coefficient-wise
locations and scales. An `intercept`/`slope` list gives separate role-wise
orders. The recovery fit receives the identical coefficient-wise distribution,
including a common global scale for a bare regularised-horseshoe declaration.

Both simulation entry points accept `formulaEvent = NULL`. This defines a
nested longitudinal mixed-model data-generating process: event data and
association terms are absent, and the scheduled longitudinal histories are
not truncated by an internally generated event time.

For example,
`marker_weights = list(intercept = 1, family = "normal")` fixes the common
marker-weight location at one. Replacing the numeric intercept by
`prior_normal(mu = 1, scale = 1)` draws one common location for a shared set or
one location per term-specific set. Both compact and term-indexed forms are
stored in `truth`. The `family` field governs only centred unit-scale marker
departures and therefore accepts a family rather than fixed coefficients.

The remaining population quantities are grouped in the same truth object.
`basehaz` declares a hazard function, formula or parametric baseline family;
`assoc_coef` contains the coefficients corresponding to the association terms
selected by `assoc`; and `re_params` contains ordinary random-effect covariance
truths. When the standard deviations of a random-effect block are omitted,
the simulator draws one vector according to

\[
\tau_r\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\operatorname{Exponential}(1).
\]

When its correlation matrix is omitted, the simulator draws

\[
L_\Omega\sim\operatorname{LKJCholesky}(\eta),\qquad
\Omega=L_\Omega L_\Omega^\top,
\]

where `eta` is supplied by `lkj = prior_lkj(eta)`. These distributions are
identical to the `exponential(1)` scale priors and
`lkj_corr_cholesky(lkj_eta)` correlation priors in the Stan longitudinal
submodel. The population scale vector and correlation matrix are each drawn
once; conditional random effects are then sampled for their allocation units.

`jm_prior()` is reserved for fitting distributions and rejects fixed
coefficient values. The recovery call stored in `truth$recovery` uses the
usual component default when a generating coefficient was fixed. A
`prior_*()` declaration used in `jm_truth()` is retained as the corresponding
recovery prior. Known marker-weight offsets and the Dirichlet concentration
for baseline class probabilities are structural quantities rather than
coefficient priors.

Let \(C_j\) be the class of allocation unit \(j\). The simulator first draws

\[
C_j\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(\boldsymbol{\pi}_j)
\]

and then, for every selected packed coordinate \(r\),

\[
Z_{jr}\mid C_j=g
\sim
D(\mu_{gr},s_{gr}).
\]

The fitted Stan programme evaluates the marginal density

\[
p(\boldsymbol Z_j)
=
\sum_{g=1}^{G}
\pi_{jg}
\prod_{r=1}^{K}
p_D(Z_{jr}\mid\mu_{gr},s_{gr})
\]

with `log_sum_exp`. Thus the discrete simulation and marginalised fitting
programme describe the same probability model.

The ordinary covariance transformations are applied only after component
sampling:

\[
\boldsymbol u_i=L_u\boldsymbol z_{u,i},
\qquad
\boldsymbol v_d=L_v\boldsymbol z_{v,d},
\qquad
L_i=L_i(\boldsymbol z_{L,i}).
\]

This ordering prevents component locations from changing meaning when the
ordinary random-effect scales change.

## Generative parameters

The fitting syntax is retained through `n_classes`, `formulaClass`,
`class_type`, `class_dimensions`, and `class_ordering`.
`class_parameters` may supply values that must be fixed exactly in a
data-generating mechanism:

- baseline class probabilities;
- component locations; and
- positive component scales.

Class-regression coefficients are declared through `truth$class$slope` under
the common numeric-fixed or `prior_*()`-generated population rule.

When one of these entries is omitted, the simulator draws it once, holds it
fixed across allocation units, and stores the realised population value in
`truth$mixture`. This is the same population-parameter rule used by the
ordinary simulator.

The class probabilities are normalised to a simplex. Formula intercepts are
excluded because the simplex already defines the zero-covariate probabilities.
Named coefficients are aligned with the class-design columns saved in the
truth record.

## Shared allocations

Subject and covariance-regression coordinates share a subject allocation.
Marker effects use a marker allocation. This is the generative counterpart of
the fitted model's single `log_sum_exp` per natural allocation unit.

## Simulation truth and blinding

The complete generative record is returned under `truth$mixture`, including
unit-specific probabilities, realised allocations, component parameters and
standardised draws. True labels are deliberately absent from `dataLong` and
`dataEvent`. Recovery studies must join them only after fitting; otherwise a
class label can inadvertently become an observed predictor.

## Recovery-study estimands

Recovery estimands include component-location and scale bias, interval
coverage, baseline and covariate-dependent class-probability recovery,
posterior probability assigned to the true class, entropy, multiclass proper
scores, outcome prediction, survival discrimination and convergence.
Simulation factors should include component overlap, rare classes, sample
size, marker count, response families, shrinkage family, censoring,
association strength and fitted class-count misspecification.

# Base JoiNMe model

For subject \(i\), marker \(d\), and time \(t\), the longitudinal predictor
is

\[
\eta_{id}(t)
=
\boldsymbol x_{id}(t)^\top\boldsymbol\beta
+
\boldsymbol z_i(t)^\top\boldsymbol u_i
+
\boldsymbol z_d(t)^\top\boldsymbol v_d
+
\boldsymbol z_{id}(t)^\top\boldsymbol w_{id}.
\]

The response follows marker-specific family \(\mathcal F_d\) with inverse link
\(g_d^{-1}\). Ancillary parameters can have their own distributional
regressions.

## Formula time basis and event integration

The time argument in every formula-derived design is the original study time.
Writing \(B(t)\) for any column produced by a linear term, polynomial,
`splines::ns()`, `splines::bs()` or another formula transformation, the fitted
predictor contains \(B(t)\) exactly as returned by `stats::model.matrix()` on
the data belonging to that submodel. This convention applies to
`formulaLong`, `formulaEvent`, `formulaDist`, both parts of `formulaVCov`,
`formulaClass` and a formula-defined baseline hazard. Knots and boundary knots
therefore retain their stated units. For example, `ns(time, knots = 1)` places
its knot at one unit of follow-up, irrespective of the largest event time.

The event calculation separately introduces the dimensionless coordinate

\[
s=\frac{t}{t_{max}},\qquad 0\leq s\leq 1,
\]

to stabilise numerical integration. This is a change of integration variable,
not a change of longitudinal model. For an event interval \((a,b]\),

\[
\int_a^b h_i(t)\,dt
=\int_{a/t_{max}}^{b/t_{max}}\widetilde h_i(s)\,ds,
\qquad
\widetilde h_i(s)=t_{max}h_i(t_{max}s).
\]

Accordingly, the numerical quadrature retains \(s_q\) as its dimensionless
coordinate. The fitted baseline intercept absorbs the constant
\(\log(t_{max})\), and reported baseline-hazard curves divide the internal
scaled-axis hazard by \(t_{max}\). Before a model matrix is formed, however,
the ordinate is returned to
\(t_q=t_{max}s_q\). The baseline-hazard basis, the ordinary Cox design and
every longitudinal formula matrix entering \(A_i(t)\) are evaluated at
\(t_q\). A current-slope association uses

\[
\frac{\eta_i\{t_{max}(s_q+\epsilon)\}-\eta_i(t_{max}s_q)}
     {t_{max}\epsilon},
\]

which is a derivative per unit of original study time. The same denominator
and the same stored formula terms are used in dynamic prediction. At the final
follow-up time, the forward ordinate is allowed to lie just beyond the event
horizon and the fitted spline's boundary extrapolation is used. Clipping the
ordinate would shorten the numerator interval whilst retaining the stated
denominator and would therefore define a different, attenuated slope.

For the Cox regression, let \(\boldsymbol W_i(t)\) denote the right-hand-side
model matrix after removing its intercept. The cause-specific event predictor
at a quadrature node is

\[
\eta^{event}_{ik}(t_q)
=\boldsymbol W_i(t_q)^\top\boldsymbol\gamma_k+A_{ik}(t_q).
\]

Thus a baseline covariate interaction such as
`treatment:ns(event_time, df = 3)` retains the subject's treatment value while
the spline columns vary over original follow-up time. The endpoint matrix
\(\boldsymbol W_i(b)\) is used for an exact-event hazard and the node matrices
\(\boldsymbol W_i(t_q)\) are used in its cumulative hazard. This does not alter
the integration rule; it gives the ordinary Cox formula its intended
time-varying coefficient.

This separation has several inferential consequences. Longitudinal
coefficients and random-effect covariance parameters are directly
interpretable in the formula's stated time units; spline coefficients do not
depend on an unrelated event horizon; a formula baseline hazard retains the
same knot locations in fitting and prediction; and new-data prediction
reproduces each fitted spline basis rather than constructing a basis on a
rescaled prediction grid. These are the ordinary R formula semantics used by
established joint-modelling packages, including JMbayes2.

The row at which the formula is evaluated remains appropriate to its
statistical level. Distributional regressions use measurement or prediction
times. Covariance regression uses its subject-level record. Class-membership
regression uses its subject or marker allocation record. The Cox and formula
baseline-hazard designs use endpoint time for endpoint quantities and
original-time quadrature ordinates for cumulative-hazard quantities. Hence the
time convention changes neither the grouping level nor the probability model
of these components.

The realised subject and marker effects are

\[
\boldsymbol u_i=L_u\boldsymbol z_{u,i},\qquad
\boldsymbol v_d=L_v\boldsymbol z_{v,d}.
\]

The nested subject-by-marker effect is

\[
\boldsymbol w_{id}
=
\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol r_w)L_i\boldsymbol z_{w,id}.
\]

The subject covariance factor is

\[
L_i=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma_i)K_i.
\]

Its standard deviations and off-diagonal factor entries have separate
subject-level regressions:

\[
\eta^{sd}_{ir}
=\alpha^{sd}_r
+\boldsymbol x_{sd,i}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta^{sd}_r
+\lambda_{m(r)}z_{L,i,m(r)},
\]

\[
\eta^{corr}_{ih}
=\alpha^{corr}_h
+\boldsymbol x_{corr,i}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta^{corr}_h
+\lambda_{m(h)}z_{L,i,m(h)}.
\]

The first predictor is mapped to a positive standard deviation by softplus or
the exponential link. The second is mapped through `tanh` to a partial
correlation used to construct the lower-triangular Cholesky correlation factor
\(K_i\). The public declaration
`formulaVCov = list(sd = ~ ..., corr = ~ ...)` supplies the two independent
designs; a single formula is their shared-design shorthand.

Within row \(r\), let \(p_{irc}=\tanh(\eta^{corr}_{i,r,c})\) for \(c<r\).
The sequential construction is

\[
K_{i,r,c}=p_{irc}\prod_{h<c}\sqrt{1-p_{irh}^2},\qquad
K_{i,r,r}=\prod_{h<r}\sqrt{1-p_{irh}^2}.
\]

Thus every row of \(K_i\) has unit norm. Together with
\(\boldsymbol\sigma_i\), this defines
\(\Sigma_i=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma_i)K_iK_i^\top\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma_i)\).
The standard-deviation regression therefore governs marginal variance, while
the partial-correlation regression governs dependence without changing that
marginal variance.

The event hazard for cause \(k\) is

\[
h_{ik}(t)
=
h_{0k}(t)
\exp\left[
\boldsymbol x_{S,i}(t)^\top\boldsymbol\gamma_k
+
A_i(t)
\right],
\]

where \(A_i(t)\) is a sum of active transformed association channels.

## Block-specific regularisation

Let \(\theta_j\) denote an intercept or slope in a scientific regression
component. The analyst may independently declare global `intercept` and
`slope` fallbacks, then replace either role within `longitudinal`, `survival`,
`vcov`, `assoc`, `functional`, `marker_weights`, or a distributional
left-hand side from `formulaDist`. Each role may use

\[
N(\mu_j,s_j^2),\qquad t_\nu(\mu_j,s_j),\qquad
\operatorname{Laplace}(\mu_j,s_j),
\]

or a regularised horseshoe. Regression-coefficient Student-\(t\) degrees of
freedom are fixed; marker-weight degrees of freedom may instead be learned
when omitted, as described below. A
scalar location or scale is repeated only within its component-role group; a
non-scalar declaration must have exactly that fitted dimension. This strict rule is important because
the model matrices are constructed dynamically and ordinary partial recycling
could silently assign a prior to the wrong scientific coefficient.

Distributional priors may repeat the family scope used by `formulaDist`.
For example, the quoted argument name
`` `sigma[family='student']` `` is canonicalised to `student_t` and governs
only the Student-$t$ sigma-regression columns. The unscoped `sigma` declaration
remains the fallback. A marker selector, such as
`` `nu[marker='m2']` ``, is resolved through the fitted marker-to-family map.
It is accepted only when that marker uniquely identifies the family-scoped
coefficient vector. When several markers share one vector, the family selector
is required because assigning different priors to a single shared coefficient
would be statistically incoherent. Selector-role groups remain separate
horseshoe groups when that prior family is requested.

For the regularised horseshoe, \(z_j\sim N(0,1)\), the local and global scales
have positive Student-\(t\) laws, and

\[
\theta_j=\mu_j+s_j\tau\widetilde\lambda_jz_j,
\qquad
\widetilde\lambda_j^2=
\frac{c^2\lambda_j^2}{c^2+\tau^2\lambda_j^2}.
\]

The finite slab \(c\) regularises exceptionally large signals. This is the
regularised construction of
[Piironen and Vehtari (2017)](https://projecteuclid.org/journals/electronic-journal-of-statistics/volume-11/issue-2/Sparsity-information-and-regularization-in-the-horseshoe-and-other-shrinkage/10.1214/17-EJS1337SI.full),
also represented in the public prior interfaces of
[brms](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/reference/horseshoe.html) and
[rstanarm](https://mc-stan.org/rstanarm/reference/priors.html), rather than an
unbounded classical horseshoe.

Standardised marker effects and marker-weight departures may select any of
these four families, but their location and ordinary scale are fixed at zero
and one. The marker covariance factor carries the marker-effect block's scale, whilst
the unit departure distribution defines the latter block's unit. A common
marker-weight location is trainable under `marker_weights$intercept`, whilst
`marker_weights$offset` supplies the known contribution. Marker-specific
departures use `marker_weights$family`; `"constant"` and `"none"` bypass both
fitted quantities and remain exactly equal to the offset. Correlation
matrices have a separate LKJ prior with concentration `eta`; they are not
forced into a scalar shrinkage family.

The fitted marker-weight intercept prior may have its own location and scale
and inherits the global intercept prior when omitted. Neither quantity is read
from `marker_weights$family`: that field controls only the distributional
shape of the centred unit-scale departures. In `jm_truth()`, a numeric
intercept fixes the data-generating population mean. A `prior_*()` intercept
draws it once and records the realised value in simulation truth.

There is deliberately no additional marker-weight standard deviation. A
marker departure enters directly on the fixed unit-scale coordinate of its
declared family. The completed weighted feature is then multiplied by the
association slope, so fitting a second free multiplier would introduce a
non-identifiable product.

For marker weights, `marker_weights$family` is normally a family label. The
Student-$t$ has two unambiguous forms: location zero and ordinary scale one
remain fixed, while the family name `"student_t"` fits a degrees-of-freedom parameter,

\[
\nu_s=2+u_s,\qquad u_s\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(2,0.1).
\]

The Gamma distribution is parameterised by shape and rate. Every marker in set
$s$ informs the same $\nu_s$, while different sets have distinct tail
parameters. Only `"student_t"` requests this fitted form.
`prior_student_t()` and `prior_student_t(df = ...)`, with `df > 2`, instead fix
the default or stated value and introduce no tail parameter. In either form, setting `mu` or
`scale` to values other than zero and one is rejected.

The six scalar association positions are ordered as total current value, total
current slope, subject-mean current value, subject-mean current slope, marker
current value and marker current slope, followed by correlation and covariance
components. The declared `assoc$slope` scale applies directly to the
log-hazard coefficient. Common marker-weight locations have their separate
intercept prior on the marker-weight scale. The `iota` coefficients govern an
optional affine transformation inside `tf()` and do not replace the
association slope. There is no additional random
association scale. This direct
meaning is especially important when eliciting priors through plausible hazard
ratios.

# Censoring and the full event likelihood

Conditional on the longitudinal random effects and the model parameters, let
\(H_i(t)\) denote the integrated all-cause hazard and let
\(S_i(t)=\exp\{-H_i(t)\}\). The event process uses the full likelihood, not the
Cox partial likelihood. A right-censored observation at \(L\) contributes
\(S_i(L)\), an exact event at \(t\) contributes
\(h_i(t)S_i(t)\), a left-censored event by \(R\) contributes
\(1-S_i(R)\), and an interval-censored event in \((L,R]\) contributes
\(S_i(L)-S_i(R)\).

`Surv(lower, upper, type = "interval2")` contains one censoring statement per
subject. For a proper interval, the R preparation produces two adjacent risk
rows. The first records known survival from zero to \(L\); the second records
failure within \((L,R]\). Their combined log contribution is

\[
-H_i(L)+\log\left[1-\exp\{-[H_i(R)-H_i(L)]\}\right]
=\log\{S_i(L)-S_i(R)\}.
\]

The lower inspection limit is not delayed entry. Event covariates on the
subject-level interval row are used over both risk contributions, whilst the
longitudinal association and baseline hazard are evaluated at the quadrature
times. Left and interval censoring presently describe one event type because
the cause is not observed inside the censoring interval.

The ordinary and latent-class entry points call the same event-likelihood
function. Class modelling changes selected random-effect distributions and
does not alter the censoring probability. Subject-level posterior log
likelihood is reconstructed by the same risk-row calculation used in fitting.

# Latent-progress model

## Component distribution

Let \(\mathcal K\) denote the selected standardised coordinates after the
requested blocks have been concatenated. For class \(g\),

\[
a_{rk}\mid C_r=g,\mu_{gk},s_{gk}
\sim D_\nu(\mu_{gk},s_{gk}),
\qquad k\in\mathcal K.
\]

The component family is selected through the existing `shrinkage` convention:

| `shrinkage` | component \(D_\nu\) |
|---:|---|
| 0 | Student-\(t\), 6 degrees of freedom |
| 1 | Laplace |
| 2 | Normal |

The finite mixture is

\[
p(\boldsymbol a_r)
=
\sum_{g=1}^{G}
\pi_g
\prod_{k\in\mathcal K}
D_\nu(a_{rk};\mu_{gk},s_{gk}).
\]

The component covariance is diagonal on the selected standardised scale. The
existing Cholesky factors remain responsible for correlations in realised
subject and marker random effects.

## Class proportions and component priors

\[
\boldsymbol\pi\sim
\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\boldsymbol\alpha_\pi),
\]

\[
s_{gk}\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(1).
\]

By default, Stan orders only the first selected random-intercept location
across classes. Slope and other location coordinates remain unrestricted.
`class_ordering = "probability"` instead orders the baseline class
probabilities, and `"none"` imposes no order. There are no anchor values or
public anchor-scale controls.

`formulaClass` optionally regresses membership on allocation-unit covariates.
The simplex supplies the intercept. One formula uses class \(G\) as the
reference category; a list of \(G\) formulae supplies separate, compact
class-specific predictors and defaults to no ordering.
`jm_prior(class = list(baseline_prob = ..., slope = ...))` supplies
\(\boldsymbol\alpha_\pi\) and an independent
Normal, fixed-degrees-of-freedom Student-t, Laplace, or regularised horseshoe
prior for the regression coefficients. Coefficient-specific locations and
scales follow subject-domain then marker-domain design order.

## Two-dimensional default

For an available block dimension \(q\), the default selected coordinates are

\[
\{1,\ldots,\min(2,q)\}.
\]

The one-dimensional special case is legitimate and is reported as such.
`class_dimensions` permits an explicit alternative.

# Four class types

## Subject effects

`class_type = "subject"` replaces the distribution of selected
\(\boldsymbol z_{u,i}\) coordinates. This is the most direct latent progression
model when the first two coordinates are a subject intercept and slope.

## Marker effects

`class_type = "marker"` replaces the distribution of selected
\(\boldsymbol z_{v,d}\) coordinates. The allocation unit is a marker. Survival
associations are not reparameterised; the class-specific marker trajectory can
nevertheless enter a current-value or current-slope association.

## Correlation effects

`class_type = "corr"` replaces selected off-diagonal correlation coordinates
of \(\boldsymbol z_{L,i}\). The coordinate indices refer to correlations only;
Stan maps them to their positions in the packed lower triangle.

## Variance--covariance effects

`class_type = "vcov"` replaces selected lower-triangular coordinates of
\(\boldsymbol z_{L,i}\), including scale coordinates. It classes subject
covariance profiles and does not assign a component distribution to every
\(\boldsymbol z_{w,id}\) innovation. `corr` and `vcov` cannot be selected
together because they describe the same latent block.

# Shared allocations and the meaning of \(G\)

The subject allocation domain contains `"subject"`, `"corr"`, and `"vcov"`.
The marker allocation domain contains `"marker"`.

For a combined subject-domain request:

\[
p(\boldsymbol z_{u,i},\boldsymbol z_{L,i})
=
\sum_{g=1}^G
\pi_g
p_g(\boldsymbol z_{u,i})
p_g(\boldsymbol z_{L,i}).
\]

The same \(g\) is used in both factors. Thus \(G=3\) gives three joint
subject-progress classes, not nine combinations.

If an subject block and a marker block are selected together, both use the
same \(G\) labels and \(\boldsymbol\pi\), but their posterior allocations are
reported over their natural units. This avoids the incoherent notion that an
subject and a marker share one observed allocation unit.

# Marginalisation in Stan

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo requires a differentiable continuous parameter space.
For allocation unit \(r\), Stan adds

\[
\log\sum_{g=1}^G
\exp\left\{
\log\pi_g+\log p_g(\boldsymbol a_r)
\right\}.
\]

Generated quantities calculate

\[
p_{rg}
=
\frac{\pi_gp_g(\boldsymbol a_r)}
{\sum_{h=1}^G\pi_hp_h(\boldsymbol a_r)}.
\]

These are conditional class probabilities for each posterior draw. The
reported probability is the posterior mean of \(p_{rg}\), with a credible
interval. A maximum-probability class is retained only for convenient tables
and plots.

# Exact replacement of the ordinary prior

The Stan model first applies the established ordinary prior. The mixture block
then adds

\[
\log p_{\mathrm{mix}}(\boldsymbol a_r)
-
\log p_{\mathrm{ordinary}}(\boldsymbol a_r).
\]

For subject and covariance-regression standardised effects, the ordinary
denominator is Normal. For marker effects, the denominator is the raw density
declared in `jm_prior(marker = ...)`: Student-t, Normal or Laplace as selected,
and standard Normal for a regularised-horseshoe raw coefficient. The latter
retains its local/global scale transformation downstream. This matching
subtraction makes the construction an exact prior replacement.

If formula-scoped random-effect weights are present, the relevant log-density
terms are weighted consistently in the numerator and denominator.

# Survival associations under latent classes

The base association decomposition is unchanged.

- Mean channels use fixed plus subject effects.
- Marker channels use marker plus subject-by-marker effects.
- Total channels add mean and marker parts.
- Correlation and covariance channels use summaries of \(L_i\).

Weighted marker aggregation follows:

\[
\bar f_{a,i}(t)
=
\frac{1}{D}
\sum_{d=1}^D
\omega_{ad}^{\mathrm{eff}}
f_a\{r_{aid}(t)\}.
\]

For an estimated weight set $s$, the effective marker weight is decomposed as

\[
\omega^{\mathrm{eff}}_{sd}
=\omega^{(0)}_{sd}+\mu_{\omega,s}+z_{sd},
\qquad d=1,\ldots,D.
\]

The common location $\mu_{\omega,s}$ is inferred jointly from all markers in
the set and is governed by `marker_weights$intercept`. It is therefore analogous
to a population intercept. The departure $z_{sd}$ has location zero and scale
one under the selected `marker_weights$family` and enters the effective weight
without another multiplier.
The value $\omega^{(0)}_{sd}$ is the known `marker_weights$offset`. Its vector
may be wholly named by marker or wholly unnamed in fitted marker order, but it
cannot be partly named. For unshared association terms, `offset` may be a named
collection containing one complete vector per active term.
This separation permits a non-zero learned average weight and direct
marker-specific heterogeneity. The association coefficient multiplies the
completed weighted feature. Its magnitude is informed by between-marker
contrast under the unit-scale departure law. Its non-negative orientation
removes the equivalent solution obtained by reversing the coefficient and all
weights, whilst retaining the common location in every effective weight. The
logical `marker_weights$shared` declaration selects the structure. Shared
association terms use one common location; term-specific sets use one location
per active weighted association term. For `cv_marker` and `cs_marker`, a common
weight shift multiplies the average centred marker trajectory. That average can
be close to zero, particularly with many markers, so the common location may
receive little likelihood information and its explicit intercept prior should
reflect scientific knowledge.

For Student-$t$ departures,

\[
\delta_{sd}\mid\nu_s\sim t_{\nu_s}(0,1),\qquad
\nu_s=2+u_s,\quad u_s\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(2,0.1).
\]

This moving degrees of freedom is used only for the family name `"student_t"`;
all markers within a set contribute to its posterior. The departure family
does not accept a `prior_*()` declaration.

Transformation occurs before marker averaging. The common weight location is
not class-specific: latent classes act through the requested random-effect
blocks, whilst the population marker-weight mean is shared and estimated from
the full marker collection.

Non-reference association coefficients remain common unless the underlying
ordinary model specifies otherwise. The mixture acts through its random-effect
or weight distribution; it does not introduce an undocumented class-specific
association coefficient.

The general posterior summary keeps this hierarchy compact. Declared
marker-specific offsets appear in the summary header. For every shared or
term-specific fitted set, the marker-weight table reports its common location
and the posterior root-mean-square realised departure. The hierarchy is

\[
\omega_{sd}=\omega^{(0)}_{sd}+\mu_{\omega,s}
+z_{sd}.
\]

The selected `marker_weights$family` governs the centred unit-scale
$z_{sd}$. The displayed `SD weight` is
$\{D^{-1}\sum_d z_{sd}^{2}\}^{1/2}$ in each posterior draw and is not a model
parameter. `marker_weights()` and `coef(fit)$assoc` return individual effective
weights, `fixef()` returns the common location, and `ranef(fit)$assoc` returns the centred
marker-specific departure
\(\omega_{sd}-\omega^{(0)}_{sd}-\mu_{\omega,s}\). These association tables
include `assoc_term`, so a shared
set appears once whereas term-specific sets retain their association labels.
The `coef()` table identifies the marker in `term` and omits a duplicate
`marker` column.
The `fixef()` table places longitudinal, event-process, and marker-weight
population quantities together, whilst retaining `component`, `event`, and
`assoc_term` identifiers. Consequently, an unshared marker-weight mean remains
attached to the association term whose hazard contribution it centres, and
event-regression coefficients remain distinguishable under competing events.

# Longitudinal estimands

## Class centre

`mean_per_class` evaluates the inverse link after inserting component locations
for the selected random-effect blocks which enter the longitudinal location.
It answers:

> What trajectory is implied by the centre of this latent component at the
> chosen covariate profile?

## Marginal within class

`marginal_per_class` draws from the fitted within-component distribution and
then applies the inverse link. It answers:

> What response-scale trajectory is expected after acknowledging
> within-component random-effect variation?

These estimands are not interchangeable under a non-linear inverse link.

## Covariance class

If covariance regression receives a latent-class distribution, the dedicated display reconstructs the
covariance matrix for every class and posterior draw over the covariance
covariate grid. Every \(G\) curve appears in the same component panel, with a
separate returned plot for each marker.

The covariance-regression loading is coordinate-specific. If \(m\) indexes one
packed lower-triangular coordinate, \(\lambda_m\) is a non-negative scalar and
the full collection \(\boldsymbol\lambda\) is a vector of length
\(M_{\mathrm{cov}}\). In vector notation its action is
\(\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\lambda)\boldsymbol z_{L,i}\), rather than a
dense loading matrix. In the ordinary model, \(\lambda_m\) is the residual
standard deviation of the untransformed covariance predictor. Under class
\(g\), the latent contribution has location
\(\lambda_m\mu_{gm}\) and distributional scale \(\lambda_ms_{gm}\); the
positive diagonal link or off-diagonal `tanh` mapping is applied
afterwards.

Observed-covariate effects are deliberately separate from this latent
loading. `formulaVCov$sd` creates one design for the standard-deviation
predictors and `formulaVCov$corr` creates another for off-diagonal K entries.
Their coefficient blocks receive independent `vcov$sd` and
`vcov$corr` intercept and slope prior declarations. A single formula is canonicalised to two
identical formulae, so the ordinary, mixture, simulation and prediction paths
still have one interface contract.

# Longitudinal-only likelihood

When both event arguments are `NULL`, the implementation creates a private
event scaffold for common design construction, then sends zero event indicators
and zero integration limits to Stan. The event contribution is exactly

\[
0-\int_0^0h_i(s)\,ds=0.
\]

No survival information enters inference. Association terms and marker-weight
classes are disallowed. Event prediction and discrimination methods explain
that no event process was fitted, while longitudinal prediction and diagnostics
remain inherited.

# Software interface

The fitted hierarchy is:

```text
JoiNMeFit
└── JoiNMeMixFit

JoiNMeDynPred
└── JoiNMeMixDynPred
```

The following established methods remain available:

- `summary()`, `print()`, `plot()`;
- `predict()` and dynamic-prediction summaries;
- `posterior_draws()`, `extract()`, `fixef()`, `ranef()`, and `vcov()`;
- `posterior_linpred()`, `posterior_epred()`, and `posterior_predict()`;
- fitted-subject conditional prediction through `reuse_fitted_re = TRUE` in
  those prediction methods, `conditional_effects()`, and
  `conditional_contrast()`;
- draw-level conditional estimands through `summary = FALSE`, returned as a
  tidy data frame with `.draw`, `.value`, `estimand__`, and the associated
  scientific descriptors;
- `pp_check()`, `diagnosis()`, and `mcmc_plot()`;
- `loo()`, `waic()`, and `elpd()`;
- `concordance()`, `tvROC()`, and `tvAUC()` for joint fits;
- `assoc()` and `posterior_assoc()`.

For longitudinal conditional effects and contrasts, the `population` and
`marginal_marker` estimands average the selected marker trajectories within
each posterior draw and therefore report one curve per condition. Population
trajectories exclude marker-level deviations, whereas marker-marginal
trajectories include them. The marker-specific inverse link precedes either
average. The `marker` estimand alone retains a separate curve for every marker.

Mixture-specific additions are:

- `posterior_class()` for fitted units and dynamically predicted subjects;
- direct plotting of a `posterior_class()` result using posterior mean
  probabilities and central intervals;
- `type = "class_membership"`;
- `estimand = "mean_per_class"`;
- `estimand = "marginal_per_class"`;
- `type = "covariance_class"`;
- class-specific association trajectories.

`posterior_assoc()` distinguishes a coefficient from its realised class
contribution. The coefficient and marker weights remain common unless the
model explicitly states otherwise. When a selected class block changes the
longitudinal or covariance feature entering an association, the method appends
a compact class-by-reference-value table using `Estimate`, `Est.Error`,
`Q2.5`, `Q97.5`, `Rhat`, `ess_bulk` and `ess_tail`. Irrelevant class blocks do
not cause duplicated class rows.

The mixture summary distinguishes five inferential objects. Baseline class
probabilities are evaluated at zero-valued centred class covariates. Component
locations and within-class scales describe the selected standardised latent
random-effect coordinates and are reported in separate tables. The
class-membership regression reports estimated multinomial-logit contrasts;
for a shared class formula, the final class is the zero-coefficient reference.
If one allocation domain has no fitted class-regression coefficient
(`P_class_subject = 0` or `P_class_marker = 0`), Stan stores a zero-length
vector and no posterior coefficient variable is produced for that domain.
Summary and prediction reporting therefore omit that regression block by
construction.
The allocation table then reports the posterior distribution of the
draw-specific expected class count and the maximum-probability hard count,
without reproducing every unit-by-class row, which remains available through
`posterior_class()`. The reported estimate, standard error, central interval,
R-hat and effective sample sizes are stored in distinct numeric columns because component
scales and probabilities need not have symmetric posterior distributions.

# Limitations

The implementation uses diagonal component scales on the selected standardised
coordinates. Correlation is retained through the underlying random-effect
Cholesky factors, but the component distribution does not add a second freely
estimated correlation matrix.

Intercept or baseline-probability ordering removes the corresponding label
permutation but does not guarantee scientifically meaningful separation. With
`class_ordering = "none"`, permutation-invariant summaries and careful
posterior inspection are particularly important.

Class-specific marginal longitudinal curves integrate the selected component
distribution. Covariance classes may primarily manifest through dispersion
rather than a shifted conditional mean.

Dynamic predictions inherit the fitted joint model and retain mixture
metadata. More importantly, dynamically sampled coordinates use the fitted
draw-specific component probabilities, locations and scales. The new
subject's history therefore updates a probability vector over classes;
the software does not treat their class as known. Combined compatible blocks
continue to contribute to one allocation density rather than independent
labels.

For a subject represented during fitting, a different posterior estimand is
available. Let (b_i^{(m)}), (v^{(m)}), (w_i^{(m)}), and (L_i^{(m)})
denote realised random effects and the covariance factor in posterior draw
(m). Fitted-subject prediction evaluates the longitudinal and hazard
functionals at these paired quantities. It does not draw a second latent vector
or condition another random-effect distribution on the already observed
history. This is both computationally lighter and the appropriate conditional
estimand when inference concerns an individual whose posterior effects were
estimated in the fitted model. Unseen subjects retain the dynamic calculation
described above.

# Computational methods

Posterior inference uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with automatic
differentiation. The longitudinal and survival contributions factor by
subject conditional on the population and random-effect parameters, so the
joint log likelihood can be divided across subjects with `reduce_sum` when
within-chain parallelism is requested. This division changes only the order of
summation, not the probability model.

Cumulative hazards are evaluated by Gauss--Kronrod quadrature. For an event
interval $(L,R]$,

\[
\int_L^R h_i(t)\,dt
\approx
\frac{R-L}{2}\sum_{q=1}^{Q}w_q
h_i\!\left\{L+\frac{R-L}{2}(x_q+1)\right\}.
\]

Every longitudinal, event, distributional, covariance, class-membership and
formula baseline-hazard matrix is evaluated at the corresponding ordinate on
the original study-time scale before the event integration coordinate is
normalised. The original fitted terms, contrasts, knots and boundary knots are
retained for prediction.

Formula-defined association transformations are translated to a compact
mathematical instruction sequence shared by fitting, simulation, prediction
and plotting. Smooth monotone transformations use I-spline coefficients;
ordered piecewise-linear transformations use cumulative simplex increments.
The same fitted transformation ordinates are propagated to prediction rather
than reconstructed from new data.

For a latent-progress model, allocation indicators are analytically
marginalised. The log density for each allocation unit uses a log-sum-exp over
the $G$ component densities. The ordinary density of every selected
standardised coordinate is replaced by its mixture density, while unselected
coordinates retain their ordinary distribution. Conditional class
probabilities are calculated from the same component log densities, which
keeps fitting and posterior classification algebraically consistent.

Regression priors are assembled only after the formula dimensions and
coefficient roles are known. Intercepts and slopes retain their scientific
component labels; covariance-regression standard-deviation and correlation
coefficients retain independent orders; marker and marker-weight departures
remain on their identified standardised scales. The architecture note records
the corresponding arrays, source boundaries and prediction routes.

# Implementation audit trail

The R implementation is centred in:

```text
R/mix.R
R/mix-methods.R
R/standata.R
R/r6.R
R/plot-api.R
R/predict.R
```

The Stan implementation is centred in:

```text
inst/stan/joinme_fit_threading.stan
inst/stan/joinme_mix_fit_threading.stan
inst/stan/joinme_dynpred_threading.stan
inst/stan/joinme_mix_dynpred_threading.stan
inst/stan/joinme_fitpred_threading.stan
inst/stan/joinme_mix_fitpred_threading.stan
inst/stan/include/submodels/README.md
inst/stan/include/submodels/longitudinal/
inst/stan/include/submodels/marker_weight/
inst/stan/include/submodels/survival/
inst/stan/include/submodels/assoc/
inst/stan/include/submodels/functional/
inst/stan/include/submodels/latent_class/
inst/stan/include/etc/data/regression_prior_data.stan
inst/stan/include/etc/parameters/regression_prior_parameters.stan
inst/stan/include/etc/transformed_parameters/regression_coefficients.stan
```

Every submodel directory is itself divided into `data`, `transformed_data`,
`parameters`, `transformed_parameters`, `model`, and
`generated_quantities`. Each of these block directories has a README which
states the statistical purpose of the block and lists its fit and
dynamic-prediction fragments. There is no `full_model` pseudo-submodel: the
six master Stan files state the ordered includes directly, while genuinely
cross-submodel quantities have descriptive files under `include/etc/`. Thus a
reader interested in, for example, marker weighting or class membership can follow
`submodels/marker_weight/` from observed inputs to posterior output without
moving between unrelated block-wide source files.

The shared prior, prediction-data and likelihood modules include:

```text
inst/stan/include/etc/data/regression_prior_data.stan
inst/stan/include/etc/data/dynamic_prediction_draw_data.stan
inst/stan/include/etc/parameters/regression_prior_parameters.stan
inst/stan/include/etc/parameters/dynamic_prediction_subject_effects.stan
inst/stan/include/etc/transformed_parameters/regression_coefficients.stan
inst/stan/include/etc/model/regression_priors.stan
inst/stan/include/etc/model/fit_threaded_likelihood.stan
inst/stan/include/etc/model/dynpred_threaded_likelihood.stan
```

The ordinary programmes do not include any mixture declaration or density.
R selects one of the six entry points before compilation and filters the
sampling data against that programme's own data contract. Thus latent-class
support does not enlarge the generated ordinary Stan model.

Every submodel directory follows the data, transformed-data, parameter,
transformed-parameter, model and generated-quantity sequence. Its README gives
the statistical interpretation; every block has a further README explaining
its files and intentional empty stages. The master files preserve dependency
order explicitly. Helpers retain only calculations which are scientifically
joint, notably the event likelihood conditional on longitudinal random effects
and the corresponding dynamic prediction.

Transformation bytecode is a distinct, model-independent module:

```text
R/bytecode-interpreter.R
inst/stan/include/etc/bytecode/interpreter.stanfunctions
inst/stan/include/etc/bytecode/README.md
```

The R expression compiler consumes the module's opcode registry, and simulation
uses the same evaluator as preprocessing and plotting. The Stan implementation
mirrors the documented instruction protocol. Neither interpreter knows about
longitudinal outcomes, event processes or latent classes, which makes this
module suitable for later extraction into a separate package.

Focused regression tests are in:

```text
tests/testthat/test-latent-progress-mixture.R
```

The live architecture map is `notes/docs/architecture.md`; the statistical and
usage vignettes are under `vignettes/joinme-latent-progress-*.qmd`.
